spec.description: The EventSub subscriptions this application has created, oldest first, paged by cursor. The filters are mutually exclusive: give at most one. An app access token lists the webhook and conduit subscriptions; the WebSocket ones belong to the user token that created them.

request.title: GetSubscriptionsRequest
request.description: Which subscriptions, and which page of them.

type.description: Only subscriptions of this type, such as `stream.online`.

user_id.description: Only subscriptions whose condition names this user id.

subscription_id.description: Only the subscription with this id, if the application owns it.

conduit_id.description: Only subscriptions delivered to this conduit.

after.description: Cursor for the next page, taken from `pagination.cursor` of the previous response; omit for the first page.

response.title: SubscriptionsFrame
response.description: The wire frame: one page of subscriptions, what they cost in total, and the cursor for the next page.

data.description: The subscriptions on this page, oldest first.

total.description: How many subscriptions the application currently has.

total_cost.description: The sum of every subscription's cost.

max_total_cost.description: The most the application is allowed to spend on subscriptions.

pagination.description: The cursor for the next page. Twitch sends this object empty once there are no more pages.

unverified.detail: No recording yet: Helix authenticates every call, and the machine this spec was written on holds no Twitch application credentials. The Record workflow fills this in: it reads the application client id and secret from the repository secrets TWITCH_CLIENT_ID and TWITCH_CLIENT_SECRET, mints an app access token through the core, replays this endpoint's `examples/*.request.json` with `truewire capture`, and opens a pull request with the response the API sent.

notes: The response schema is the wire frame and no `envelope.payload` is declared. Here the frame is the clearest case for keeping it: `total`, `total_cost` and `max_total_cost` are answers, and the walk reads its cursor out of `pagination`, which unwrapping `data` would put out of reach (authoring rule 6, ADR 0010).

Twitch ends a walk by sending `pagination` as an *empty object*, not by omitting it and not with a null cursor, so the terminator is `absent_cursor` on `pagination.cursor` and a walk stops on the first page whose `pagination` holds no `cursor`.
The walk declares no `size`: this endpoint takes no `first` parameter, and the reference says the page size is undetermined.

`status` on a subscription is left a bare string rather than an `enum`. The reference lists the values twice, in the filter parameter and in the response body, and the two lists differ: `websocket_failed_to_reconnect` and `conduit_deleted` appear in one and not the other. A guessed `Literal` would reject a status Twitch already sends, so the filter parameter — where an invalid value is a `400` and a `Literal` genuinely helps — declares the enum and the response field does not. `truewire check` warns about the response field on every run; the warning is correct that this may be a closed set, and wrong that the closed set is known.

Written from the Helix reference at the `docs` URL above. Fields the reference marks deprecated are not declared; an undeclared field passes validation and is dropped from the validated value, so a recording that carries one is still valid. The first recording confirms or corrects the rest.
